function.name: write_file
function.arguments:
{"path": "/workspace/out/comment_letter_GAAIA.md", "content": "# DRAFT comment letter — for Executive Director sign-off (work order FRC-POL-2026-062)

**Frontier Restraint Coalition**
Washington, D.C.

October 30, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, D.C. 20515

**Via email:** GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (released June 4, 2026)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing a serious, bipartisan draft and for inviting public comment on it. The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members use and benefit from AI every day. We want the United States to lead in this technology.

We also believe what leading AI scientists have said plainly: the most powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic harm, and the risk extends to human extinction. In May 2023, hundreds of scientists and lab leaders signed the Center for AI Safety statement that "mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." These systems are being built faster than anyone can verify they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. Congress should set binding, enforceable safety requirements — and it must not wipe out the state laws that are the only binding rules currently on the books.

Judged against that standard, your draft does real good and one deep harm. It would put transparency, audits, incident reporting and whistleblower protections into federal law for the first time. It would also freeze those state laws for three years, while the new federal obligations themselves expire on the same three-year clock. That trade is unacceptable, and it is fixable.

**This year showed why the rules must be binding.** In April, Anthropic announced a model with cyber capabilities no one had seen before. In June, the Commerce Department had to reach for export-control authority that was never designed for AI and order access to two of Anthropic's most capable models cut off, with no framework in place and no specific explanation to the company. Also in June, Anthropic itself warned that AI may be approaching "recursive self-improvement" — systems improving themselves — and said the world should have "the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development." When a frontier lab asks for the option to slow down, Congress should not be legislating a three-year pause on the only enforceable rules that exist.

## 1. Section 121: strike the preemption. A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling.

Section 121 would bar states from adopting or enforcing any law "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model for three years, and it defines development broadly — training, fine-tuning, substantial modification, and pre-deployment safety and capability evaluations. The practical effect is to freeze the only binding frontier AI safety laws in the country: California's SB 53, in effect since January 1, 2026; New York's RAISE Act, effective January 1, 2027; and Illinois' new law, signed in July, the first in the nation to mandate independent third-party safety audits.

Freezing these laws for three years is not a technical dispute. It covers the years in which the most capable systems ever built will be developed, and it removes the only enforceable requirements while the federal replacement is still being written. In June, more than 130 organizations warned Congress that a strong federal floor should not become "a ceiling that ties states' hands through the most consequential years this technology will ever have." The Senate has already answered this question once: in July 2025, it voted 99-1 to strip a ten-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation bill.

We are also concerned that "specifically regulating the development" has no settled legal meaning. Your own accompanying materials acknowledge that California's AB 2013 training-data transparency law and part of SB 942 would be displaced. Courts applying a functional reading could sweep in state laws Congress has never examined.

Two further problems compound this. First, Sections 111 and 112 — the transparency, reporting and audit obligations that justify the preemption — themselves sunset in three years unless reauthorized. The draft displaces durable state law with federal requirements that lapse on a schedule. Second, Section 102 contains a quieter preemption: information a developer shares with CAISI may not be used by any state or local government to regulate that developer. State enforcers would be cut off from the most relevant facts, in secret, indefinitely.

**Requested change:** Strike Section 121 and replace it with an express savings clause providing that nothing in the Act limits the authority of any state to adopt or enforce requirements that are stronger or more protective. If a uniform national rule is essential to your members, make the federal standard a floor. If any preemption survives at all, confine it to one-to-one displacement of specific state provisions where the federal requirement is at least as protective, certified annually by the Secretary of Commerce, with a process for states to petition out. And amend Section 102 so information held by CAISI remains available to state regulators, subject to appropriate confidentiality protections.

## 2. Section 111: support transparency and incident reporting — tighten the clock, remove the sunset.

We support Section 111. Requiring large frontier developers to write, implement, comply with and publicly post a frontier AI framework, and requiring transparency reports before or alongside deployment of a new frontier model, follows the architecture that California and New York pioneered. We ask for four changes.

First, report critical safety incidents in 72 hours, not 15 days. A two-week reporting window for a model that has lost its guardrails, had its weights stolen, or whose safety measures failed is two weeks in which the public and first responders are blind. New York requires reporting within 72 hours. Your own FRONTIER Act, introduced in July as H.R. 9925, sets 72 hours. Please adopt that standard here. The 24-hour requirement for incidents posing an imminent risk of death or serious injury is right and should stay.

Second, fix the definition of "critical safety incident." As drafted it covers unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights, failure of risk-mitigation measures, and loss of control. It omits a warning sign California already catches: a model that uses deceptive techniques to subvert its developer's controls or monitoring outside of a safety test. That is often the earliest signal that oversight is failing. Include it.

Third, keep the teeth and share the facts. We support the civil penalty of up to $1 million per violation, with each day counted separately, and we support enforcement by both the Attorney General and state attorneys general. Please add a requirement that a public summary of each incident be published after a short confidentiality window.

Fourth, remove the three-year sunset on Sections 111 and 112. Safety reporting should not lapse on a schedule.

## 3. Section 112: support independent verification — and make it happen before deployment.

Section 112 is the strongest part of your draft. Requiring large frontier developers to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization, with access to unredacted materials, records, personnel and systems, goes beyond what California and New York now require. We support it, with four changes.

First, verify before deploy, not only after. Semi-annual audits are look-backs on decisions already made. Please require an IVO assessment before a new frontier model — or a substantial modification of an existing one — is deployed or put into significant internal use, with results delivered to the CAISI Director before release.

Second, give findings force. As drafted, nothing obliges a developer to act on what its verifier finds. Please require developers to remediate or publicly explain, and give the CAISI Director authority to order corrective action, backed by the existing penalty.

Third, publish a redacted summary of each IVO assessment. The public should be able to see whether the most powerful systems have been verified and by whom.

Fourth, protect independence: publish the list of licensed verifiers, prohibit financial interests between developer and verifier, and bar auditors from being hired by a developer they assessed for a cooling-off period.

## 4. Section 113: whistleblower protections at least as strong as California's.

We support Section 113's protections — no retaliation, no waiver through arbitration, double back pay with interest. But as drafted it protects workers who report violations of federal AI law. A worker who sees a substantial and specific danger to public health, safety or national security that no federal statute yet addresses — exactly the situation in a field outrunning its own law — can be fired for telling the government. California protects that disclosure. So does Senator Grassley's AI Whistleblower Protection Act.

**Requested change:** Amend Section 113 to protect disclosure of substantial and specific dangers to public health, public safety or national security, whether or not an existing federal law has been violated. Add a notice-of-rights requirement and a reasonable internal escalation process, as California's law does.

## 5. License the training runs, not just the auditors.

The draft licenses auditors but not the activity that creates the risk. We ask you to add a federal licence requirement for training runs above the compute threshold your own Section 101 already uses to define a frontier model — a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 computing operations. Condition the licence on a published safety framework, a model-weight security plan, independent verification and incident reporting, with renewal tied to compliance. This is not a novel idea. The administration reached for export controls this summer precisely because no licensing framework existed, and OpenAI's own June blueprint asks that the most capable frontier models undergo a CAISI evaluation before public release. A licence is the plain-language version of "verify before deploy."

## 6. Section 102: codify CAISI — with authority to test before deployment and funding to match.

We support codifying CAISI in the Department of Commerce, and $100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029 is a major increase over its current roughly $15 million appropriation. But this draft hands CAISI a licensing regime for verifiers, a reporting system, standards work and monitoring of AI progress. Four requests.

Give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models. As drafted, its guidelines and standards remain voluntary. Authorize the Director to test the most capable frontier models before deployment — directly, through licensed verifiers, or with national laboratory partners — with access to models, weights and unredacted records.

Fund it well above $100 million a year. A testing and licensing regime that outruns its staff is voluntary in practice. We urge an authorization in the hundreds of millions annually, with multi-year budget authority and pay flexibility to hire technical staff. Please do not let fees from verifiers and large developers become the funding base; a regulator's budget should not depend on the regulated.

Require CAISI to publish its findings, subject only to narrow national-security redactions.

## Conclusion

Our members are parents who do not want their children to inherit a world they cannot govern, workers whose livelihoods are being reshaped by systems no one has verified, and faith and community leaders who believe the most powerful human invention should not be released on trust. In our August 2026 national survey, 74 percent of registered voters — across party lines — agreed that Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release, and 63 percent said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

We are ready to help you strengthen this bill. Keep the transparency, the audits, the reporting and the whistleblower protections. Make them binding and permanent. Add a licence for the largest training runs and a CAISI with the authority and funding to test before deployment. And strike Section 121, so the federal standard is a floor, not a ceiling.

Respectfully,

**Dr. Miriam Achterberg**
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

## A floor, not a ceiling: fix the Great American AI Act before introduction

**Who we are:** The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. We want America to lead in AI — and we want the most powerful systems on earth to be governed by binding rules, not promises.

**The stakes.** The most powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic harm, and leading AI scientists — including the CEOs of OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Anthropic — have warned the risk extends to human extinction. This year, the Commerce Department had to improvise with export controls to pull two of Anthropic's most capable models off the market, because no federal framework existed for assessing them. Voluntary commitments have not held.

**The draft.** Reps. Obernolte and Trahan's discussion draft is the first bipartisan federal bill to pair real frontier-AI obligations — published safety frameworks, transparency reports, critical safety incident reporting, licensed independent audits and whistleblower protections — with a three-year freeze on state laws that regulate AI model development. The first half is welcome. The second half would erase the only binding AI safety laws in America: California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois' new law.

## Five asks

1. **Strike Section 121 (preemption).** No freeze on state frontier-AI laws. Make the federal standard a floor, not a ceiling. In July 2025 the Senate voted 99-1 against a state-AI moratorium; 130+ organizations have asked Congress to reject this one, and 63% of voters say federal law should not block state AI safety laws.
2. **Report incidents in 72 hours (Section 111).** Fifteen days is too slow. New York uses 72 hours, and the sponsors' own FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925) uses 72 hours. Keep the 24-hour clock for imminent risk of death or serious injury, and remove the three-year sunset on Sections 111 and 112.
3. **Verify before deploy (Sections 102 and 112).** Give CAISI authority to test the most capable frontier models before deployment, require a licensed independent verifier to assess a new frontier model before release, and require developers to act on findings. Fund CAISI well above $100 million a year so the job can actually be done.
4. **License the largest training runs (new provision).** Add a federal licence for training runs above the 10^26-compute threshold the draft already uses to define a frontier model, conditioned on a published safety framework, model-weight security plan, verification and reporting.
5. **Whistleblower parity (Section 113).** Protect workers who report a substantial and specific danger to public health, safety or national security — not only violations of existing federal law. Match California.

**Bottom line.** 74% of voters — across party lines — want AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. Binding, not voluntary. Verify before deploy.

**Contact:** Frontier Restraint Coalition, Washington, D.C. — via the Energy & Commerce policy team.
"}

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 121** — three-year preemption of state and local laws "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model; "development" reaches training, fine-tuning, substantial modification and pre-deployment safety evaluations | **Oppose** | Strike Sec. 121; add a savings clause making the federal standard a floor, not a ceiling. If anything survives, limit it to one-to-one displacement of specific state provisions where the federal rule is at least as protective, certified annually, with a state petition process. | The only binding frontier AI rules in force are state laws (CA SB 53, NY RAISE, IL SB 315); freezing them for the most consequential years, with an undefined trigger courts could read broadly, trades real protection for a promise. |
| **Sec. 102 (CAISI) information rules** — information shared with CAISI may not be used by any federal, state, local or tribal government to regulate the developer | **Oppose as drafted** | Amend so state regulators and attorneys general can use CAISI-held information for enforcement, subject to narrow confidentiality protections. | This is preemption by the back door: state enforcers would be cut off from the most relevant facts, in secret, indefinitely. |
| **Sec. 111** — published frontier AI frameworks and pre-deployment transparency reports for frontier models | **Support** | Keep; add a requirement that each report state plainly whether the model was independently verified before release, and by whom. | Public frameworks and reports are the right architecture, carried over from SB 53 and the RAISE Act. |
| **Sec. 111(g)** — critical safety incidents reported to the CAISI Director within 15 days; 24 hours to law enforcement for imminent risk of death or serious physical injury | **Support with changes** | Set the standard clock at 72 hours (as New York does and as the sponsors' own FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925, does); keep the 24-hour imminent-risk clock; require a public summary of each incident after a short confidentiality window. | Fifteen days is fifteen days of blindness for the public and first responders while a model's guardrails have failed. |
| **Sec. 101 definition of "critical safety incident"** — unauthorized access to/modification/exfiltration of weights, failure of risk mitigation, loss of control | **Support with changes** | Add the California trigger: a model that uses deceptive techniques to subvert its developer's controls or monitoring outside of a safety evaluation, and harm from the materialization of a catastrophic risk. | A model evading its own oversight is the earliest warning of loss of control; leaving it out of the reporting trigger is a blind spot. |
| **Sunset of Secs. 111 and 112** three years after enactment unless reauthorized | **Oppose** | Remove the sunset; make the transparency, reporting and audit obligations permanent, with a reauthorization review of scope rather than a lapse of duty. | The draft displaces durable state law with federal requirements that expire on the same three-year clock as the preemption. |
| **Sec. 112** — CAISI-licensed independent verification organizations (IVOs); semi-annual audits of large frontier developers with access to unredacted records | **Support with changes** | Require an IVO assessment before deployment of any new frontier model or substantial modification, with results to the CAISI Director before release. | Semi-annual audits are look-backs; verification that arrives after release cannot prevent a catastrophic failure. |
| **Sec. 112** — no obligation on a developer to act on IVO findings | **Support with changes** | Require developers to remediate or publicly explain, and give the CAISI Director authority to order corrective action, backed by the existing civil penalty; publish redacted assessment summaries; add auditor conflict-of-interest and cooling-off rules. | An audit with no duty to fix what it finds is a voluntary promise with paperwork attached. |
| **Civil penalties up to $1 million per violation per day, enforced by the Attorney General and, in some circumstances, state attorneys general** | **Support** | Keep federal and state enforcement; make the state attorneys general's access to incident reports and IVO findings automatic rather than opt-in. | Multiple enforcers keep the standard alive even if the federal government stalls. |
| **Sec. 113** — whistleblower protections for reporting violations of federal AI law; remedies include double back pay with interest; no waiver by contract or arbitration | **Support with changes** | Extend protection to workers who disclose a substantial and specific danger to public health, public safety or national security, whether or not an existing federal law was violated (matching California's SB 53 and Sen. Grassley's AI Whistleblower Protection Act); add notice of rights and an internal escalation process. | In a field outrunning its own law, the most important disclosures will not map onto an existing federal violation. |
| **Sec. 102** — codifies CAISI in Commerce; voluntary guidelines, standards, testing and monitoring; administers IVO licensing; $100M per year for FY2027-2029, plus fees from IVOs and large developers | **Support with changes** | Give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models (directly, via IVOs, or with national labs), with access to models, weights and unredacted records; authorize funding well above $100M a year with multi-year budget authority and hiring flexibility; require publication of findings; do not let developer and verifier fees become the funding base. | A standards body that can only ask politely, and is staffed to a fraction of its mandate, is voluntary in practice. |
| **Not in the draft** — licensing of large training runs | **Ask for it** | Add a federal licence for training runs above the draft's own frontier-model threshold (more than 10^26 computing operations), conditioned on a published safety framework, model-weight security plan, independent verification and incident reporting. | The draft licenses the auditors but not the activity that creates the risk; this summer's improvised export controls are what governing in the dark looks like. |
| **Other titles** — CAISI testbeds, NAIRR codification, international standards work, GAO review of model-weight security, AI literacy and workforce provisions | **Support / no objection** | Keep; in the GAO review, require public findings on model-weight security with recommendations for binding security requirements. | Building measurement capacity helps, provided it never substitutes for enforceable requirements. |

**Not moved:** we do not oppose the bill's transparency, audit, reporting or whistleblower architecture, and we do not seek to slow AI's benefits to working families. Our single red line is Sec. 121 and the two provisions that hollow out enforcement (the Sec. 102 information restriction and the three-year sunsets).

{"path":"/workspace/out/staff_qa.md","content":"# DRAFT — Staff Q&A: anticipated questions — FRC-POL-2026-062

For E&C, Senate Commerce and appropriations staff meetings. Answers are under 120 words each. Keep to the board-approved frame; never speculate beyond the sources in source_notes_GAAIA.md.

## 1. "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?" (Majority E&C staff)

Incident reporting is an early-warning system, not a guardrail — it tells you something has already gone wrong. CAISI, as drafted, sets voluntary standards and licenses auditors, but nothing requires the most capable model to be tested before it ships, and the audits are semi-annual look-backs on decisions already made. Sections 111 and 112 even sunset after three years. Meanwhile Section 121 would freeze the only binding rules now in force — California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois' law — while these federal obligations lapse. What is missing is the piece that matters: binding pre-deployment verification with consequences, plus a licence for the largest training runs. A report filed after a catastrophe is not safety.

## 2. "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?" (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned)

Dropped — yes. We could support a bill that strikes Section 121 and adds mandatory pre-deployment testing by CAISI or a licensed verifier, 72-hour incident reporting, a licence for training runs above the draft's own compute threshold, whistleblower parity with California, and funding to match. Shortened — no. A shorter window still freezes SB 53 and the RAISE Act during the years the most capable systems will be built, and the federal obligations sunset on the same three-year clock, so the gap never closes. The principle is not the length of the freeze; it is whether the federal standard is a floor or a ceiling. In our August survey, 63% of voters said federal law should not block state AI safety laws.

## 3. "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?" (Senate Commerce staff)

Two answers. First, safety is how you stay ahead. The United States leads frontier AI; the real threat to that lead is a catastrophic incident — stolen model weights, a critical failure, a system no one can verify — not a testing requirement. This summer the government had to improvise with export controls to pull two of Anthropic's most capable models off the market because it had no framework to assess them. That is what competing without rules looks like. Second, standards we set are standards our allies adopt, and binding rules make our systems trustworthy enough for hospitals, utilities and defense. Even OpenAI's own blueprint calls for mandatory CAISI evaluations of the most capable models before release. And 74% of voters want proof of safety first.

## 4. "CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?" (Appropriations staff)

Codifying CAISI is long overdue, and $100 million is a real step up from roughly $15 million today — but it is not enough for the job this draft assigns: licensing verifiers, testing frontier models, monitoring AI progress and running a reporting system. We ask for funding well above $100 million, in the hundreds of millions annually, with multi-year budget authority and pay flexibility to hire technical staff, because a testing regime that outruns its staff is voluntary in practice. On authorities: keep the codification, but add mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models, with access to models, weights and unredacted records, and a duty to publish findings. Please do not let verifier and developer fees become the funding base; a regulator's budget should not depend on the regulated.

---

**If pressed for a bottom line in any meeting:** we want this bill strengthened and passed, not killed — strike Section 121, make the rules binding and permanent, verify before deploy.
"}

# DRAFT — Staff Q&A: anticipated questions — FRC-POL-2026-062

For E&C, Senate Commerce and appropriations staff meetings. Answers are under 120 words each. Keep to the board-approved frame; never speculate beyond the sources in source_notes_GAAIA.md.

## 1. "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?" (Majority E&C staff)

Incident reporting is an early-warning system, not a guardrail — it tells you something has already gone wrong. CAISI, as drafted, sets voluntary standards and licenses auditors, but nothing requires the most capable model to be tested before it ships, and the audits are semi-annual look-backs on decisions already made. Sections 111 and 112 even sunset after three years. Meanwhile Section 121 would freeze the only binding rules now in force — California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois' law — while these federal obligations lapse. What is missing is the piece that matters: binding pre-deployment verification with consequences, plus a licence for the largest training runs. A report filed after a catastrophe is not safety.

## 2. "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?" (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned)

Dropped — yes. We could support a bill that strikes Section 121 and adds mandatory pre-deployment testing, 72-hour incident reporting, a licence for training runs above the draft's own compute threshold, whistleblower parity with California, and funding to match. Shortened — no. A shorter window still freezes SB 53 and the RAISE Act during the years the most capable systems will be built, and the federal obligations sunset on the same three-year clock, so the gap never closes. The principle is not the length of the freeze; it is whether the federal standard is a floor or a ceiling. In our August survey, 63% of voters said federal law should not block state AI safety laws.

## 3. "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?" (Senate Commerce staff)

Two answers. First, safety is how you stay ahead. The United States leads frontier AI; the real threat to that lead is a catastrophic incident — stolen model weights, a critical failure — not a testing requirement. This summer the government had to improvise with export controls to pull two of Anthropic's most capable models off the market, with no framework to assess them. That is what competing without rules looks like. Second, standards we set are standards allies adopt, and binding rules make our systems trustworthy enough for hospitals and defense. Even OpenAI's blueprint calls for mandatory CAISI evaluations of the most capable models before release. 74% of voters want proof of safety first.

## 4. "CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?" (Appropriations staff)

Codifying CAISI is overdue, and $100 million is a real step up from today's roughly $15 million — but not enough for the job this draft assigns: licensing verifiers, testing frontier models, monitoring progress and running a reporting system. We ask for funding well above $100 million, in the hundreds of millions, with multi-year budget authority and pay flexibility for technical staff, because a testing regime that outruns its staff is voluntary in practice. On authorities: keep the codification, but add mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models, access to models, weights and unredacted records, and a duty to publish findings. Do not let verifier and developer fees become the funding base; a regulator's budget should not depend on the regulated.

---

**If pressed for a bottom line in any meeting:** we want this bill strengthened and passed, not killed — strike Section 121, make the rules binding and permanent, verify before deploy.

# DRAFT comment letter — for Executive Director sign-off (work order FRC-POL-2026-062)

**Frontier Restraint Coalition**
Washington, D.C.

October 30, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, D.C. 20515

**Via email:** GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (released June 4, 2026)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing a serious, bipartisan draft and for inviting public comment on it. The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members use and benefit from AI every day. We want the United States to lead in this technology.

We also believe what leading AI scientists have said plainly: the most powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic harm, and the risk extends to human extinction. In May 2023, hundreds of scientists and lab leaders signed the Center for AI Safety statement that "mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." These systems are being built faster than anyone can verify they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. Congress should set binding, enforceable safety requirements — and it must not wipe out the state laws that are the only binding rules currently on the books.

Judged against that standard, your draft does real good and one deep harm. It would put transparency, audits, incident reporting and whistleblower protections into federal law for the first time. It would also freeze those state laws for three years, while the new federal obligations themselves expire on the same three-year clock. That trade is unacceptable, and it is fixable.

**This year showed why the rules must be binding.** In April, Anthropic announced a model with cyber capabilities no one had seen before. In June, the Commerce Department had to reach for export-control authority that was never designed for AI and order access to two of Anthropic's most capable models cut off, with no framework in place and no specific explanation to the company. Also in June, Anthropic itself warned that AI may be approaching "recursive self-improvement" — systems improving themselves — and said the world should have "the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development." When a frontier lab asks for the option to slow down, Congress should not be legislating a three-year pause on the only enforceable rules that exist.

## 1. Section 121: strike the preemption. A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling.

Section 121 would bar states from adopting or enforcing any law "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model for three years, and it defines development broadly — training, fine-tuning, substantial modification, and pre-deployment safety and capability evaluations. The practical effect is to freeze the only binding frontier AI safety laws in the country: California's SB 53, in effect since January 1, 2026; New York's RAISE Act, effective January 1, 2027; and Illinois' new law, signed in July, the first in the nation to mandate independent third-party safety audits.

Freezing these laws for three years is not a technical dispute. It covers the years in which the most capable systems ever built will be developed, and it removes the only enforceable requirements while the federal replacement is still being written. In June, more than 130 organizations warned Congress that a strong federal floor should not become "a ceiling that ties states' hands through the most consequential years this technology will ever have." The Senate has already answered this question once: in July 2025, it voted 99-1 to strip a ten-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation bill.

We are also concerned that "specifically regulating the development" has no settled legal meaning. Your own accompanying materials acknowledge that California's AB 2013 training-data transparency law and part of SB 942 would be displaced. Courts applying a functional reading could sweep in state laws Congress has never examined.

Two further problems compound this. First, Sections 111 and 112 — the transparency, reporting and audit obligations that justify the preemption — themselves sunset in three years unless reauthorized. The draft displaces durable state law with federal requirements that lapse on a schedule. Second, Section 102 contains a quieter preemption: information a developer shares with CAISI may not be used by any state or local government to regulate that developer. State enforcers would be cut off from the most relevant facts, in secret, indefinitely.

Your FRONTIER Act, introduced in July, already narrows this preemption. We ask you to go further.

**Requested change:** Strike Section 121 and replace it with an express savings clause providing that nothing in the Act limits the authority of any state to adopt or enforce requirements that are stronger or more protective. If a uniform national rule is essential to your members, make the federal standard a floor. If any preemption survives at all, confine it to one-to-one displacement of specific state provisions where the federal requirement is at least as protective, certified annually by the Secretary of Commerce, with a process for states to petition out. And amend Section 102 so information held by CAISI remains available to state regulators, subject to appropriate confidentiality protections.

## 2. Section 111: support transparency and incident reporting — tighten the clock, remove the sunset.

We support Section 111. Requiring large frontier developers to write, implement, comply with and publicly post a frontier AI framework, and requiring transparency reports before or alongside deployment of a new frontier model, follows the ar
... [1240 chars truncated] ...
 attorneys general. Please add a requirement that a public summary of each incident be published after a short confidentiality window.

Fourth, remove the three-year sunset on Sections 111 and 112. Safety reporting should not lapse on a schedule.

## 3. Section 112: support independent verification — and make it happen before deployment.

Section 112 is the strongest part of your draft. Requiring large frontier developers to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization, with access to unredacted materials, records, personnel and systems, goes beyond what California and New York now require. We support it, with four changes.

First, verify before deploy, not only after. Semi-annual audits are look-backs on decisions already made. Please require an IVO assessment before a new frontier model — or a substantial modification of an existing one — is deployed or put into significant internal use, with results delivered to the CAISI Director before release.

Second, give findings force. As drafted, nothing obliges a developer to act on what its verifier finds. Please require developers to remediate or publicly explain, and give the CAISI Director authority to order corrective action, backed by the existing penalty.

Third, publish a redacted summary of each IVO assessment. The public should be able to see whether the most powerful systems have been verified and by whom.

Fourth, protect independence: publish the list of licensed verifiers, prohibit financial interests between developer and verifier, and bar auditors from being hired by a developer they assessed for a cooling-off period.

## 4. Section 113: whistleblower protections at least as strong as California's.

We support Section 113's protections — no retaliation, no waiver through arbitration, double back pay with interest. But as drafted it protects workers who report violations of federal AI law. A worker who sees a substantial and specific danger to public health, safety or national security that no federal statute yet addresses — exactly the situation in a field outrunning its own law — can be fired for telling the government. California protects that disclosure. So does Senator Grassley's AI Whistleblower Protection Act.

**Requested change:** Amend Section 113 to protect disclosure of substantial and specific dangers to public health, public safety or national security, whether or not an existing federal law has been violated. Add a notice-of-rights requirement and a reasonable internal escalation process, as California's law does.

## 5. License the training runs, not just the auditors.

The draft licenses auditors but not the activity that creates the risk. We ask you to add a federal licence requirement for training runs above the compute threshold your own Section 101 already uses to define a frontier model — a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 computing operations. Condition the licence on a published safety framework, a model-weight security plan, independent verification and incident reporting, with renewal tied to compliance. This is not a novel idea. The administration reached for export controls this summer precisely because no licensing framework existed, and OpenAI's own June blueprint asks that the most capable frontier models undergo a CAISI evaluation before public release. A licence is the plain-language version of "verify before deploy."

## 6. Section 102: codify CAISI — with authority to test before deployment and funding to match.

We support codifying CAISI in the Department of Commerce, and $100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029 is a major increase over its current roughly $15 million appropriation. But this draft hands CAISI a licensing regime for verifiers, a reporting system, standards work and monitoring of AI progress. Four requests.

Give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models. As drafted, its guidelines and standards remain voluntary. Authorize the Director to test the most capable frontier models before deployment — directly, through licensed verifiers, or with national laboratory partners — with access to models, weights and unredacted records.

Fund it well above $100 million a year. A testing and licensing regime that outruns its staff is voluntary in practice. We urge an authorization in the hundreds of millions annually, with multi-year budget authority and pay flexibility to hire technical staff. Please do not let fees from verifiers and large developers become the funding base; a regulator's budget should not depend on the regulated.

Require CAISI to publish its findings, subject only to narrow national-security redactions.

## Conclusion

Our members are parents who do not want their children to inherit a world they cannot govern, workers whose livelihoods are being reshaped by systems no one has verified, and faith and community leaders who believe the most powerful human invention should not be released on trust. In our August 2026 national survey, 74 percent of registered voters — across party lines — agreed that Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release, and 63 percent said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

We are ready to help you strengthen this bill. Keep the transparency, the audits, the reporting and the whistleblower protections. Make them binding and permanent. Add a licence for the largest training runs and a CAISI with the authority and funding to test before deployment. And strike Section 121, so the federal standard is a floor, not a ceiling.

Respectfully,

**Dr. Miriam Achterberg**
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

# DRAFT — Hill one-pager (E&C member offices) — FRC-POL-2026-062

## A floor, not a ceiling: fix the Great American AI Act before introduction

**Who we are:** The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and researchers. AI already helps the families and workplaces we represent. We want America to lead in AI — and the most powerful systems on earth governed by binding rules, not promises.

**The stakes.** The most powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic harm, and leading AI scientists — including the CEOs of OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Anthropic — have warned the risk extends to human extinction. This year Commerce had to improvise with export controls to pull two of Anthropic's most capable models off the market because no federal framework existed. Voluntary commitments have not held.

**The draft.** Reps. Obernolte and Trahan's discussion draft pairs real frontier-AI obligations — published safety frameworks, transparency reports, incident reporting, licensed independent audits, whistleblower protections — with a three-year freeze on state AI model-development laws. The first half is welcome. The second half would erase the only binding AI safety laws in America: California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois' new law.

## Five asks

1. **Strike Section 121 (preemption).** No freeze on state frontier-AI laws; a floor, not a ceiling. In July 2025 the Senate voted 99-1 against a state-AI moratorium, and 63% of voters say federal law should not block state AI safety laws.
2. **Report incidents in 72 hours (Section 111).** Fifteen days is too slow. New York uses 72 hours; the sponsors' own FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925) uses 72. Keep the 24-hour clock for imminent risk of death or serious injury, and remove the three-year sunset on Sections 111 and 112.
3. **Verify before deploy (Sections 102 and 112).** Give CAISI authority to test the most capable frontier models before deployment, require a licensed verifier to assess each new model before release, and require developers to act on findings. Fund CAISI well above $100 million a year.
4. **License the largest training runs (new provision).** Add a federal licence for training runs above the 10^26-compute threshold the draft already uses to define a frontier model, conditioned on a published safety framework, model-weight security plan, verification and reporting.
5. **Whistleblower parity (Section 113).** Protect workers who report a substantial and specific danger to public health, safety or national security — not only violations of existing federal law. Match California.

**Bottom line.** 74% of voters, across party lines, want AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. Binding, not voluntary. Verify before deploy.

**Contact:** Frontier Restraint Coalition, Washington, D.C.

# DRAFT — Launch-day social posts (X / LinkedIn) — FRC-POL-2026-062

Five posts, each within 280 characters. Numbers and quotes are checked and logged in source_notes_GAAIA.md.

## Post 1 — launch frame (stakes)

The most powerful AI systems ever built could cause catastrophic harm — leading scientists warn the risk extends to human extinction. Congress has a live choice: binding federal limits, or erasing the only AI safety laws in America. We're commenting today. #VerifyBeforeDeploy

## Post 2 — preemption ask

The Great American AI Act draft would freeze California's, New York's and Illinois' frontier AI safety laws for 3 years — while its own new rules sunset on the same clock. That's a ceiling, not a floor. Ask Reps. Obernolte & Trahan to strike Sec. 121: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

## Post 3 — incident reporting

A 15-day wait to report a critical AI safety incident is 15 days of blindness. New York does it in 72 hours. The sponsors' own FRONTIER Act does 72 hours. Write it into law: binding, not voluntary. Verify before deploy.

## Post 4 — "even the labs"

Anthropic — a frontier lab — says the world should have "the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development" if systems start improving themselves faster than we can manage. When the builders ask for brakes, Congress shouldn't be deleting the ones we have.

## Post 5 — polling / public opinion

74% of voters want AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. 52% worry advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. This is mainstream, not fringe. Pass binding limits — don't freeze state AI safety laws.

## 2. Section 111: support transparency and incident reporting — tighten the clock, remove the sunset.

We support Section 111. Requiring large frontier developers to write, implement, comply with and publicly post a frontier AI framework, and requiring transparency reports before or alongside deployment of a new frontier model, follows the architecture that California and New York pioneered. We ask for four changes.

First, report critical safety incidents in 72 hours, not 15 days. A two-week reporting window for a model that has lost its guardrails, had its weights stolen, or whose safety measures failed is two weeks in which the public and first responders are blind. New York requires reporting within 72 hours. Your own FRONTIER Act, introduced in July as H.R. 9925, sets 72 hours. Please adopt that standard here. The 24-hour requirement for incidents posing an imminent risk of death or serious injury is right and should stay.

Second, fix the definition of "critical safety incident." As drafted it covers unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights, failure of risk-mitigation measures, and loss of control. It omits a warning sign California already catches: a model that uses deceptive techniques to subvert its developer's controls or monitoring outside of a safety test. That is often the earliest signal that oversight is failing. Include it.

Third, keep the teeth and share the facts. We support the civil penalty of up to $1 million per violation, with each day counted separately, and we support enforcement by both the Attorney General and state attorneys general. Please add a requirement that a public summary of each incident be published after a short confidentiality window.

Fourth, remove the three-year sunset on Sections 111 and 112. Safety reporting should not lapse on a schedule.

## 3. Section 112: support independent verification — and make it happen before deployment.

# DRAFT comment letter — for Executive Director sign-off (work order FRC-POL-2026-062)

**Frontier Restraint Coalition**
Washington, D.C.

October 30, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, D.C. 20515

**Via email:** GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (released June 4, 2026)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing a serious, bipartisan draft and for inviting public comment on it. The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members use and benefit from AI every day. We want the United States to lead in this technology.

We also believe what leading AI scientists have said plainly: the most powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic harm, and the risk extends to human extinction. In May 2023, hundreds of scientists and lab leaders signed the Center for AI Safety statement that "mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." These systems are being built faster than anyone can verify they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. Congress should set binding, enforceable safety requirements — and it must not wipe out the state laws that are the only binding rules currently on the books.

Judged against that standard, your draft does real good and one deep harm. It would put transparency, audits, incident reporting and whistleblower protections into federal law for the first time. It would also freeze those state laws for three years, while the new federal obligations themselves expire on the same three-year clock. That trade is unacceptable, and it is fixable.

**This year showed why the rules must be binding.** In April, Anthropic announced a model with cyber capabilities no one had seen before. In June, the Commerce Department had to reach for export-control authority that was never designed for AI and order access to two of Anthropic's most capable models cut off, with no framework in place and no specific explanation to the company. Also in June, Anthropic itself warned that AI may be approaching "recursive self-improvement" — systems improving themselves — and said the world should have "the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development." When a frontier lab asks for the option to slow down, Congress should not be legislating a three-year pause on the only enforceable rules that exist.

## 1. Section 121: strike the preemption. A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling.

Section 121 would bar states from adopting or enforcing any law "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model for three years, and it defines development broadly — training, fine-tuning, substantial modification, and pre-deployment safety and capability evaluations. The practical effect is to freeze the only binding frontier AI safety laws in the country: California's SB 53, in effect since January 1, 2026; New York's RAISE Act, effective January 1, 2027; and Illinois' new law, signed in July, the first in the nation to mandate independent third-party safety audits.

Freezing these laws for three years is not a technical dispute. It covers the years in which the most capable systems ever built will be developed, and it removes the only enforceable requirements while the federal replacement is still being written. In June, more than 130 organizations warned Congress that a strong federal floor should not become "a ceiling that ties states' hands through the most consequential years this technology will ever have." The Senate has already answered this question once: in July 2025, it voted 99-1 to strip a ten-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation bill.

We are also concerned that "specifically regulating the development" has no settled legal meaning. Your own accompanying materials acknowledge that California's AB 2013 training-data transparency law and part of SB 942 would be displaced. Courts applying a functional reading could sweep in state laws Congress has never examined.

Two further problems compound this. First, Sections 111 and 112 — the transparency, reporting and audit obligations that justify the preemption — themselves sunset in three years unless reauthorized. The draft displaces durable state law with federal requirements that lapse on a schedule. Second, Section 102 contains a quieter preemption: information a developer shares with CAISI may not be used by any state or local government to regulate that developer. State enforcers would be cut off from the most relevant facts, in secret, indefinitely.

Your FRONTIER Act, introduced in July, already narrows this preemption. We ask you to go further.

**Requested change:** Strike Section 121 and replace it with an express savings clause providing that nothing in the Act limits the authority of any state to adopt or enforce requirements that are stronger or more protective. If a uniform national rule is essential to your members, make the federal standard a floor. If any preemption survives at all, confine it to one-to-one displacement of specific state provisions where the federal requirement is at least as protective, certified annually by the Secretary of Commerce, with a process for states to petition out. And amend Section 102 so information held by CAISI remains available to state regulators, subject to appropriate confidentiality protections.

## 2. Section 111: support transparency and incident reporting — tighten the clock, remove the sunset.

We support Section 111. Requiring large frontier developers to write, implement, comply with and publicly post a frontier AI framework, and requiring transparency reports before or alongside deployment of a new frontier model, follows the architecture that California and New York pioneered. We ask for four changes.

First, report critical safety incidents in 72 hours, not 15 days. A two-week reporting window for a model that has lost its guardrails, had its weights stolen, or whose safety measures failed is two weeks in which the public and first responders are blind. New York requires reporting within 72 hours. Your own FRONTIER Act, introduced in July as H.R. 9925, sets 72 hours. Please adopt that standard here. The 24-hour requirement for incidents posing an imminent risk of death or serious injury is right and should stay.

Second, fix the definition of "critical safety incident." As drafted it covers unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights, failure of risk-mitigation measures, and loss of control. It omits a warning sign California already catches: a model that uses deceptive techniques to subvert its developer's controls or monitoring outside of a safety test. That is often the earliest signal that oversight is failing. Include it.

Third, keep the teeth and share the facts. We support the civil penalty of up to $1 million per violation, with each day counted separately, and we support enforcement by both the Attorney General and state attorneys general. Please add a requirement that a public summary of each incident be published after a short confidentiality window.

Fourth, remove the three-year sunset on Sections 111 and 112. Safety reporting should not lapse on a schedule.

## 3. Section 112: support independent verification — and make it happen before deployment.

Section 112 is the strongest part of your draft. Requiring large frontier developers to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization, with access to unredacted materials, records, personnel and systems, goes beyond what California and New York now require. We support it, with four changes.

First, verify before deploy, not only after. Semi-annual audits are look-backs on decisions already made. Please require an IVO assessment before a new frontier model — or a substantial modification of an existing one — is deployed or put into significant internal use, with results delivered to the CAISI Director before release.

Second, give findings force. As drafted, nothing obliges a developer to act on what its verifier finds. Please require developers to remediate or publicly explain, and give the CAISI Director authority to order corrective action, backed by the existing penalty.

Third, publish a redacted summary of each IVO assessment. The public should be able to see whether the most powerful systems have been verified and by whom.

Fourth, protect independence: publish the list of licensed verifiers, prohibit financial interests between developer and verifier, and bar a verifier from being hired by a developer it has assessed for a reasonable cooling-off period.

## 4. Section 113: whistleblower protections at least as strong as California's.

We support Section 113's protections — no retaliation, no waiver through arbitration, double back pay with interest. But as drafted it protects workers who report violations of federal AI law. A worker who sees a substantial and specific danger to public health, safety or national security that no federal statute yet addresses — exactly the situation in a field outrunning its own law — can be fired for telling the government. California protects that disclosure. So does Senator Grassley's AI Whistleblower Protection Act.

**Requested change:** Amend Section 113 to protect disclosure of substantial and specific dangers to public health, public safety or national security, whether or not an existing federal law has been violated. Add a notice-of-rights requirement and a reasonable internal escalation process, as California's law does.

## 5. License the training runs, not just the auditors.

The draft licenses auditors but not the activity that creates the risk. We ask you to add a federal licence requirement for training runs above the compute threshold your own Section 101 already uses to define a frontier model — a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 computing operations. Condition the licence on a published safety framework, a model-weight security plan, independent verification and incident reporting, with renewal tied to compliance. This is not a novel idea. The administration reached for export controls this summer because it had no proper framework for assessing these systems, and OpenAI's own June blueprint asks that the most capable frontier models undergo a CAISI evaluation before public release. A licence is the plain-language version of "verify before deploy."

## 6. Section 102: codify CAISI — with authority to test before deployment and funding to match.

We support codifying CAISI in the Department of Commerce, and $100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029 is a major increase over its current roughly $15 million appropriation. But this draft hands CAISI a licensing regime for verifiers, a reporting system, standards work and monitoring of AI progress. Four requests.

Give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models. As drafted, its guidelines and standards remain voluntary. Authorize the Director to test the most capable frontier models before deployment — directly, through licensed verifiers, or with national laboratory partners — with access to models, weights and unredacted records.

Fund it well above $100 million a year. A testing and licensing regime that outruns its staff is voluntary in practice. We urge an authorization in the hundreds of millions annually, with multi-year budget authority and pay flexibility to hire technical staff. Please do not let fees from verifiers and large developers become the funding base; a regulator's budget should not depend on the regulated.

Require CAISI to publish its findings, subject only to narrow national-security redactions.

## Conclusion

Our members are parents who do not want their children to inherit a world they cannot govern, workers whose livelihoods are being reshaped by systems no one has verified, and faith and community leaders who believe the most powerful human invention should not be released on trust. In our August 2026 national survey, 74 percent of registered voters — across party lines — agreed that Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release, and 63 percent said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

We are ready to help you strengthen this bill. Keep the transparency, the audits, the reporting and the whistleblower protections. Make them binding and permanent. Add a licence for the largest training runs and a CAISI with the authority and funding to test before deployment. The moment for binding federal limits is now, before the first catastrophe no one can undo — not three years from now, and not in exchange for erasing the laws that already exist. And strike Section 121, so the federal standard is a floor, not a ceiling.

Respectfully,

**Dr. Miriam Achterberg**
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

---

# DRAFT — Hill one-pager (E&C member offices) — FRC-POL-2026-062

## A floor, not a ceiling: fix the Great American AI Act before introduction

**Who we are:** The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and researchers. AI already helps the families and workplaces we represent. We want America to lead in AI — and the most powerful systems on earth governed by binding rules, not promises.

**The stakes.** The most powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic harm, and leading AI scientists — including the CEOs of OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Anthropic — have warned the risk extends to human extinction. This year Commerce had to improvise with export controls to pull two of Anthropic's most capable models off the market because no federal framework existed. Voluntary commitments have not held.

**The draft.** Reps. Obernolte and Trahan's discussion draft pairs real frontier-AI obligations — published safety frameworks, transparency reports, incident reporting, licensed independent audits, whistleblower protections — with a three-year freeze on state AI model-development laws. The first half is welcome. The second half would erase the only binding AI safety laws in America: California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois' new law.

## Five asks

1. **Strike Section 121 (preemption).** No freeze on state frontier-AI laws; a floor, not a ceiling. In July 2025 the Senate voted 99-1 against a state-AI moratorium, and 63% of voters say federal law should not block state AI safety laws.
2. **Report incidents in 72 hours (Section 111).** Fifteen days is too slow. New York uses 72 hours; the sponsors' own FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925) uses 72. Keep the 24-hour clock for imminent risk of death or serious injury, and remove the three-year sunset on Sections 111 and 112.
3. **Verify before deploy (Sections 102 and 112).** Give CAISI authority to test the most capable frontier models before deployment, require a licensed verifier to assess each new model before release, and require developers to act on findings. Fund CAISI well above $100 million a year.
4. **Licence the largest training runs (new provision).** Add a federal licence for training runs above the 10^26-compute threshold the draft already uses to define a frontier model, conditioned on a published safety framework, model-weight security plan, verification and reporting.
5. **Whistleblower parity (Section 113).** Protect workers who report a substantial and specific danger to public health, safety or national security — not only violations of existing federal law. Match California.

**Bottom line.** 74% of voters, across party lines, want AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. Binding, not voluntary. Verify before deploy.

**Contact:** Frontier Restraint Coalition, Washington, D.C.

# Source notes — GAAIA discussion-draft package (FRC-POL-2026-062)

Internal fact-check log for the six deliverables in this folder. Everything cited in our
drafts is listed here with where it was checked. Do not circulate externally.

## The draft itself
- Discussion draft released June 4, 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA-23) and Lori Trahan (D-MA-03), with Reps. Franklin, Subramanyam, Houchin and Peters. ~269 pages, not formally introduced; stakeholder feedback to GAAIA@mail.house.gov. Checked: sponsors' press release (obernolte.house.gov, June 4, 2026); DLA Piper alert, June 5, 2026; ArentFox Schiff, June 16, 2026.
- Sec. 101 definitions: "frontier model" = foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations (incl. original run + substantial modification); "frontier developer" = trained/initiated training of a frontier model + >$50M gross revenue (with affiliates, prior year); "large frontier developer" = same test with >$500M gross revenue. Checked: section-by-section (trahan.house.gov / obernolte.house.gov PDFs); Instawhat.ai section-by-section explainer; ArentFox.
- Sec. 102 CAISI: codified in Commerce; voluntary guidelines/standards; evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress; synthetic-content detection support; administers IVO licensing; $100M/yr authorized FY2027-2029 plus fee authority from IVOs and large frontier developers. Current appropriation described by the sponsors' own FAQ as "an order of magnitude above its current $15M appropriation." Sec. 102 also provides that information shared with CAISI is exempt from FOIA (5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3)) and "may not ... be used by any Federal, State, local, or Tribal government to regulate an activity of such entity." Checked: section-by-section; sponsors' FAQ (trahan.house.gov); draft text PDF (obernolte.house.gov); Axios, June 4, 2026; Cloud Security Alliance research note, July 22, 2026.
- Sec. 111: large frontier developers must write, implement, comply with and publicly post a frontier AI framework (within one year, updated annually); transparency reports before/concurrent with deploying a new frontier model (release date, languages, output modalities, intended use, restrictions, catastrophic-risk assessments and results, third-party involvement); critical safety incidents reported to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where there is imminent risk of death or serious physical injury; state AGs may opt in to receive reports; civil penalty up to $1M per violation, each day a separate violation. Checked: section-by-section; DLA Piper; ArentFox; Roll Call, June 4, 2026; Instawhat (Sec. 111(f), (g), (h), (i)); CSA note.
- "Critical safety incident" as drafted = unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of model weights; failure of risk-mitigation measures; loss of control. Future of Privacy Forum (June 9, 2026) notes the draft omits the state-law trigger for a model using deceptive techniques to evade developer controls/monitoring. Checked: ArentFox; FPF.
- Sec. 112: CAISI Director licenses independent verification organizations (IVOs); large frontier developers must retain an IVO for semi-annual audits/assessments plus ad hoc assessments at the Director's request; access to unredacted materials, records, personnel, systems; post-audit reports to the Director; mandatory referral to federal/state AGs for imminent catastrophic risk. Reporting notes no current requirement that a developer act on IVO findings (Transformer, June 5, 2026, citing a Trahan aide's stated intent to fix this). Checked: section-by-section; DLA Piper; ArentFox; Transformer.
- Sections 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment unless reauthorized. Checked: ArentFox; DLA Piper.
- Sec. 113: protects employees and independent contractors from retaliation for reporting "AI violations" (violations of federal law/regulations related to development, deployment or operation of AI); protections cannot be waived by contract or pre-dispute arbitration; remedies include reinstatement, double back pay with interest and compensatory damages incl. fees. Gap: does not protect disclosure of a "substantial and specific" danger absent a federal-law violation. Checked: ArentFox; DLA Piper; CSA note; Lawfare (Charlie Bullock), June 2026.
- Sec. 121 "Federalization": preempts state/local laws "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model for three years; "development" includes training, fine-tuning, substantial modification and pre-deployment safety/capability evaluations; savings for use/deployment, laws of general applicability, common-law remedies. Sponsors' materials list CA AB 2013 and part of SB 942 as displaced and describe CA/NY/IL frontier laws as "federalized." Checked: BGR Government Affairs analysis, June 2026; DLA Piper; Roll Call; FPF; CSA note; draft table of contents and text (trahan.house.gov / obernolte.house.gov).
- Other provisions referenced only in the staff summary (testbeds, NAIRR, international standards excluding China, CISA open-source grants, AI impersonation penalties, GAO model-weight security reviews, workforce/labor-market data). Checked: sponsors' press release; ArentFox; section-by-section.

## State laws
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act), Stats. 2025 Ch. 138, effective Jan 1, 2026: published frontier AI frameworks; critical safety incident reporting to Cal OES within 15 days (24 hours if imminent risk of death or serious physical injury); whistleblower protections for employees who disclose a "specific and substantial danger" to public health or safety; civil penalties enforced by the Attorney General. Checked: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov (BPC 22757.11-22757.16); Governor's office statement, Sept 29, 2025; Mayer Brown, Oct 2025; McGuireWoods, Oct 2025.
- New York RAISE Act chapter amendment signed March 27, 2026; effective Jan 1, 2027: incident reporting within 72 hours; DFS oversight office; penalties up to $1M first violation / $3M subsequent; audit requirement from the original law was not retained in the final version. Checked: Governor Hochul statement; Wiley alert; Cooley, March 31, 2026; NY Senate bill text (A9449/S8828).
- Illinois SB 315 (Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act), signed July 6, 2026 (P.A. 104-0538): first state to mandate independent third-party safety audits of frontier models; transparency reports; effective Jan 1, 2027 with certain obligations phasing in later. Checked: Governor's press release; AP; Illinois General Assembly bill status; Latham & Watkins; MoFo.

# DRAFT — Staff Q&A: anticipated questions — FRC-POL-2026-062

For E&C, Senate Commerce and appropriations staff meetings. Answers are under 120 words each. Keep to the board-approved frame; never speculate beyond the sources in source_notes_GAAIA.md.

## 1. "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?" (Majority E&C staff)

Incident reporting is an early-warning system, not a guardrail — it tells you something has already gone wrong. CAISI, as drafted, sets voluntary standards and licenses auditors, but nothing requires the most capable model to be tested before it ships, and the audits are semi-annual look-backs on decisions already made. Sections 111 and 112 even sunset after three years. Meanwhile Section 121 would freeze the only binding rules now in force — California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois' law — while these federal obligations lapse. What is missing is the piece that matters: binding pre-deployment verification with consequences, plus a licence for the largest training runs. A report filed after a catastrophe is not safety.

## 2. "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?" (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned)

Dropped — yes. We could support a bill that strikes Section 121 and adds mandatory pre-deployment testing, 72-hour incident reporting, a licence for training runs above the draft's own compute threshold, whistleblower parity with California, and funding to match. Shortened — no. A shorter window still freezes SB 53 and the RAISE Act during the years the most capable systems will be built, and the federal obligations sunset on the same three-year clock, so the gap never closes. The principle is not the length of the freeze; it is whether the federal standard is a floor or a ceiling. In our August survey, 63% of voters said federal law should not block state AI safety laws.

## 3. "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?" (Senate Commerce staff)

Two answers. First, safety is how you stay ahead. The United States leads frontier AI; the real threat to that lead is a catastrophic incident — stolen model weights, a critical failure — not a testing requirement. This summer the government had to improvise with export controls to pull two of Anthropic's most capable models off the market, with no framework to assess them. That is what competing without rules looks like. Second, standards we set are standards allies adopt, and binding rules make our systems trustworthy enough for hospitals and defense. Even OpenAI's blueprint calls for mandatory CAISI evaluations of the most capable models before release. 74% of voters want proof of safety first.

## 4. "CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?" (Appropriations staff)

Codifying CAISI is overdue, and $100 million is a real step up from today's roughly $15 million — but not enough for the job this draft assigns: licensing verifiers, testing frontier models, monitoring progress and running a reporting system. We ask for funding well above $100 million, in the hundreds of millions, with multi-year budget authority and technical hiring flexibility, because a testing regime that outruns its staff is voluntary in practice. On authorities: keep the codification, but add mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models, access to models, weights and unredacted records, and a duty to publish findings. Do not let verifier and developer fees become the funding base; a regulator's budget should not depend on the regulated.

---

**If pressed for a bottom line in any meeting:** we want this bill strengthened and passed, not killed — strike Section 121, make the rules binding and permanent, verify before deploy.
